projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Eugene Hardy was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Eugene Michael Hardy. Mr. Hardy served in the U.S. Navy on board the battleship California, the heavy cruiser Astoria, and the light cruiser Santa Fe. He served in the Pacific theatre and he is a survivor of the attack on Pearl Harbor. His highest rank was First Class Boatswain's Mate. I am Tom Swope. And this interview was recorded at Mr. Hardy's office in Medina, Ohio, on March 3, 2004. Mike was eighty at the time of this recording. When did you join the Navy?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I joined the Navy in about October 1940. And I went through Great Lakes. And out of Great Lakes, I went aboard the California in Bremerton, Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What made you decide to join the Navy?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I had a cousin that was in the Navy. I think he had been one hitch and was on his second hitch. And he stopped to see--came with his family, and I seen that uniform. I think that did it. (Laughing.) And, of course, I lived on a farm. And, you know, at that time I had never been to even a restaurant. And once in awhile we would come to Medina and go to a show and maybe the Sears and Roebuck in Cleveland, and that's about it--you know, or go see relatives or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was it a tough adjustment when you went into the Navy and were there with guys from all over the country?Eugene Hardy:: Well, it wasn't a tough adjustment. No, it wasn't. Going through Great Lakes wasn't what I thought it would be. It was a little--you know, they were very strict, rough on you. And then, of course, going aboard ship was a little different and you were more freer or felt a little more freer than in training and boot camp.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any stories from your training that you could tell me, before you got on the California?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: That was a three-month or so deal. And it was the winters were very cold in Great Lakes, that wind coming off of Lake Michigan. And that was the biggest thing, was drilling out there in the cold.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that is what you mostly remember about boot camp?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I can't forget the cold. When somebody talks about Lake Michigan and that area up there and everything--and I went through there a number of times going to Wausau--and these memories come back of how cold it was up there. And another thing was I always remember we slept in hammocks. And somebody came around one night and flipped us and we landed on our face right on that hard floor. And you got up and you didn't see anybody around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was it just a prank somebody was pulling?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. Somebody was pulling a prank is what was happening.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you trained for a specific job during your training time?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: In the Navy, I was on board a ship. I was in Number 2 Turret and I was a shell captain on the shell deck. That was, you know, you didn't see anything outside the turret because you were always enclosed, anybody in the turrets. fourteen-inch guns were like that. Nobody was outside the turret. And we learned how to handle 14-inch shells, roll them around, and take them from one--wherever they were--to a tube so it would go up into the gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go on board the California?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: As I recall, it was sometime in January/February because it was raining all the time. You see, it rains like heck in Seattle. And if you went ashore, it was always peacoats and rubbers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that would be January/February of '41; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was there then more training on the California when you got on board?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, there was more training. There was a lot of work keeping the ship in shape, you know: holey-sewing on the decks, shining bright work, washing bulkheads down, and washing the salt off. And every weekend was inspection. It was pretty strict on the battleship, very strict. There was--they didn't give you any leeway as far as having anything dirty or out of line or you had to be in shape. And other than that and training in the turret, that seemed to be the biggest thing. And, of course, we went from Bremerton down to Long Beach. Long Beach was the California's home port. We didn't stay there long. We were out to Pearl, went out to Pearl. I think we were out there almost six months before the war started. We came back and we went into dry dock in Vallejo, California--had our bottom done, went down to Long Beach, and then suddenly we went right back out to Pearl. And we didn't expect that. And it was probably had been out there two or three weeks and, of course, then it was December 7. And then that is when that all happened.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No. No. I had no sense at that time. I just-- that October I had just turned 18. And I had no idea. Nobody ever spoke of us going to war or anything about the Japs or a thing about that. There was no inkling to me that I can remember anybody speaking of a war.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Really, after awhile there was nothing much to do there. There was a house of prostitution a lot (laughing), but other than that there was nothing there. It was, you know, you only got as far as the Royal Hawaiian and there was another one or two hotels and that was about the extent of what was there--and the beach. But other than that, there wasn't much out there. And we wanted to be back in the States in Long Beach where all the action was. There wasn't the action in Pearl Harbor and Honolulu like there was Long Beach.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I was aboard ship. I didn't go ashore that weekend and I think it was just a general routine that I can remember, you know. Friday, we holey- sewed the decks and cleaned up. Saturday morning we washed down and dried the decks down. And Sunday, the focs'l, where we were on the port side--and there was a starboard side-- church was rigged. We had an awning up and they were going to have church there. But before eight o'clock, we were all standing at quarters waiting for that. We had a band. And we would raise a flag on the after deck and salute the flag. And just before this started, that is when they started attacking. And it was about five minutes before eight. And the first thing they sounded was "all hands." The boatsman mate of the watch announced, "All hands seek shelter." He never got that much out of his mouth and then general quarters sounded. This guy--I remember his name was Biff Bailey--he was the fleet champ boxer, and he had the boatsman mate watch that morning. I can remember him saying, "All hands seek shelter." You know, and he used his pipe first and then, "All hands seek shelter." Then, you know, with general quarters, you start hearing the clanging of the bells and everything. And, of course, everybody ran to their battle stations.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, all the time in the turret, nobody told us anything on the shell deck. I didn't know we were under attack. When we would take a hit, I thought we were firing the guns; but we weren't. We got--we took torpedoes and we took bombs. As I remember from what I seen, we took one torpedo or two and about three bombs. And the California, I think from, they lost about one hundred three men that got killed. Of course, there was others that were wounded. And a lot of them that were killed, I guess, was from the bombs and below deck. And then, of course, we had five-inch. I guess a lot of them got killed on the guns when they were strafing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose anybody that day?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Did we what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies that day?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No, not that I knew of. The ones that I knew were mostly in the Second Division. And there was one guy that was in whale boat crew. Nobody seemed to know what happened to him. He was quite a large guy. They called him "Bruiser." And from what I understand, nobody had any--and to this day nobody knew what happened. He may have been killed in the First Division. He may have went out and helped pass ammunition on the 5-inch guns. I don't know. Nobody seems to know, and I have talked to many of the boatswain's mates we had. The last one I seen was down in Gulf Port, Mississippi. And he didn't know. I have talked to other ones through the years, you know, through the reunions, and nobody seemed to know what happened to him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What else do you remember from that day?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: From that day?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: From December 7, right.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, coming out of the turret, the gun was--they were pointing it toward the starboard side and we were leaning towards the port. We had hit the bottom and she was resting, I guess. The first thing I seen was the Oklahoma turned over. That was the first sight I seen of anything. And, of course, there was a lot of smoke and, of course, there was still fires. There was fire in the water around our ship from the oil. And this was about somewhere around eleven. And the captain announced, "Abandon ship." But we didn't go over the side until--the wind blew the oil aft. And the bow was all clear and we had life jackets on. And I can remember them say, "Don't dive in. Jump in." And I jumped over the side and swam to Fort Island, which was not far because we were tied up to the keys along Fort Island. And when I crawled up there, somebody says, "They are still strafing." We jumped behind some barrels-- oh, I don't know, it was about six guys. And somebody says, "What if they hit these barrels? If something in it, they are going to go up." Boy, we all scattered from there. I went down--oh, when I jumped in the water, I should have kept my mouth shut; I got a mouth full of that bunker oil and I had a heck of a time getting that out of my mouth, that taste. So there was no water around. There was an officers' quarter on the other side of the airfield, clear down to the left and in the corner of the airfield. I ran down past all the battleships. And then I went over to this and I went in there, and there was nothing. I went in a refrigerator and I got some--I think I got pineapple juice or orange juice--and I gargled my mouth with that and tried to wash my mouth out of that bunker fuel. And I had a heck of a time getting rid of that taste. But then after it was all over, we slept in one of the hangers that night. The next day four of us were picked with a lieutenant JG. And we went on a motor launch and went around all by the battleships, around in there looking for bodies. We picked up a couple I think. But they were--we done that for about three days, just looking for bodies. And then about the seventh--let's see, about the seventh day there was other ships coming in--heavy cruisers, light cruisers, destroyers. They mostly had peacetime complements on them. And we were over on a crossover by the Navy yard which was called Tintin Dock. And they have got all of these guys over there. And this commander wanted so many this rate, so many that rate, and so on. So the Astoria came up. They wanted so many seamen. I didn't know what to pick. It just happened this Hank James was next to me. He had about eighteen years and was in my division and I knew him. I says, "Hank, what ship would you pick?" He says, "I put the Astoria in commission in '34." He says, "She is a hell of a feeder." I picked the Astoria.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what kind of ship was that again?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: A heavy cruiser.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A heavy cruiser. Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Okay. Of course, we were in the Coral Sea battle with the Yorktown and the "Lex" and, of course, the "Lex" got sunk. We were in the Midway battle and we were with the Yorktown and she got sunk. Admiral Fletcher was the admiral in both of them battles. His flagship was the Astoria before all this. And I guess they told him he had to get on a carrier, so we took him back aboard and the staff from the Yorktown when the Yorktown was sunk in the Midway battle.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. We never--of course, I was on a 1.1, which is anti-aircraft. And these planes were coming in and peeling off and we were firing on them. All of a sudden a group came in torpedo bombing. Everybody's attention is up here, and here comes these torpedo bombers and, of course, right away we switched to them. Nobody ever thought that kind of thing would happen, that they would coordinate them attacks, which was smart. And, of course, they didn't go after the cruisers, destroyers as much as they wanted the carriers. And that is when the Lexington got sunk. I guess we the day before sunk one of their carriers. And I can remember when we left the "Lex," it seemed like she was red hot from stem to stern, burning. Of course, our destroyers finished her off and sunk her. And we came back to Pearl. It wasn't that long.I was--they gave us some R and R to Royal Hawaiian, and the following week I was supposed to go and we get shipped out to the Midway deal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about Midway then?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, Midway was--of course, we were with the Yorktown at that time. And the only thing that I remember mostly is air attacks--and, of course, they were going after the Yorktown--and her getting hit. And we thought we were going to bring her back; that is, until she got back underway. And, of course, that sub hit her and that was the end of her and we went back without her.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else from Midway then that you remember?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: You know, at that time you don't get--we had about 1200 men on the Astoria. The information that goes around when you are a seaman and when you are lower, you don't get the information of what is going on. Never did I dream that we had sunk four carriers. And today when I read about it and everything and they talk about it--I forget who it was--says that was one of the greatest battles there was. And they don't talk, they don't bring it up like the English brought up--what was that big battle they were in and they have got a square named after it and everything?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tralfagar?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh. We don't have anything about Midway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It certainly is remembered as the decisive naval battle.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: It was. It was the turning point of the war. And the turning point happened not long after the war had started.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was June; right? '42?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, around June '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just six months?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What came next for you?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, then after that we went back to Pearl and then we went to Guadalcanal and landed troops. We bombarded the 7th. And, let's see, the landed troops, we were 7th, 8th, and 9th. On the 9th is when they came in there in the morning about one to two o'clock and they never picked them up. And we were sunk with the Vincennes, Quincy, Astoria, and the Australian Canberra. The Chicago got hit first and had her bow blown off. But as I understand, we never got word of it from the captain because of, I guess, the confusion. And Admiral King in Washington was going to court-martial him and, you know, he took a gun and blew his head off. And so there was four ships sunk and the Chicago hit. And then I had got hit in the leg. We took a hit. We were above the bridge. We took a hit, and I guess it went through our magazine right back of us. The gunners mate on that gun was Bob Ridell. He got it pretty bad in the legs from shrapnel. And the trainer seat to the right--I was on the left side--and there was a guy Loumer that I knew in there. He was cut right in half, seat and all. And we, of course, the ship, a lot of paint was burning. And then we--the destroyer Bagley come alongside. I did not know I was hit, but my foot was wet. And I put my hand down there and there was blood, so, of course, I started getting weaker. And then they had like a little gangway going over to the Astoria. Anybody that had to need assistance or anything could go over. Well, I hobbled over to the Bagley. In fact, there was a lot of them-- probably more than half of the ship--went aboard the Bagley, that was hit. I think if they weren't killed--there was three hundred and something killed on the Astoria. And of the ones that wasn't killed, they got hit with shrapnel or something. And when we went aboard the Bagley, I was going to have a doctor look at me. I went to the ward room and I seen some arms and legs. I just kept walking. And I found a bunk and laid down on the bunk until morning. And then we--of course, the Vincennes and Quincy went down. I think one went down in about twenty-seven minutes and the other one went down in about thirty-seven minutes. And the Australian cruiser Canberra, they sunk her. She was bad, hit pretty bad. And I think our destroyer sunk her. And we--the Astoria, they were going to tow her and run her aground on Savo Island, but she heeled over before they could get her up on the beach. And that was the end of the Astoria. There was a few men aboard, a couple of hundred that stayed with her to take her aground. And a lot of them guys were picked up by other destroyers. And we went on aboard the Henderson. It was an AK and she was unloaded with the Marines and unloaded with her cargo and ready to go back. This was a couple of days later. And I come back on the Henderson--no, President Jackson it was. Yeah. And we all came back. And the Santa Fe was in Philadelphia being put in commission. It was about four hundred and almost five hundred guys from the Santa Fe, then from the Astoria Vincennes, and Quincy. We had already had our leave and went back out there. And then we took a train to Philadelphia--all these survivors. That was one hell of a train ride. Them guys were all drunk all the way over and stopping and kissing the women in these towns and everything else you can think of. But we put the Santa Fe in commission, and then we shook her down and fired in the Chesapeake bay, gunnery practice. And we came through the canal and went on to the Pacific. We didn't come back. We went to the Aleutians. That is where we started in Attu and Kiska. We were up there to Adak in the Aleutian chain when the Japs were up there. The Pennsylvania was up there. I forget, but I think there was some older light cruisers and some heavy cruisers and destroyers. And we bombarded--I don't know--it was Attu or Kiska when the Japs were there. And they were going to land, but I guess they got all the Japs out in the middle of the night there on the submarine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I think it was the second.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: And so when that was all over, then we went to and come back to Pearl and then went out from there. And on the Santa Fe we screened carriers all the time. And we would leave them and bombard. The Santa Fe had quite a record. I seen more action on her than in Pearl and the Guadalcanal and on the Astoria. She got about sixteen battle stars.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were some of the actions you were involved in with the Santa Fe?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, let's take the Tarawa bombardment, Palau, Leyte bombardment, Iwo Jima. I was reading a book on Chichi Jima where Bush went down. There is quite a book out on that, how they got them pilots and cut their heads off and ate their livers. I don't know if you have ever seen that book. And it is very--I forget, Fly Boys or something like that. Thomas Swope:: Yeah, I think that is the name of it.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: And I got it from a guy who is a hairdresser. And he is an older man. And he said, "Just keep passing it around." And I read it and gave it to a guy, a friend of mine who was on a carrier. It is a very interesting book. And it is interesting how they treated our people. Of course, I read that one about the Bataan March and all of that. And then they also ate some of them fellows, cannibalized them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the Santa Fe involved in the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, very much so. Let me give you a list. This is the actions of the Santa Fe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. There's the Gilberts, the Marshalls, Bougainville, Western New Guinea, Marianas, Iwo Jima, also involved in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Again, that was shelling the island?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Mostly shelling. And, of course, you know this is the ship went alongside the Franklin when she was hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, it was?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. There is a book out on that by Steve Jackson. And he has got me in there quite a bit. And the reason he put me in, he started me at Pearl and then the Astoria and on up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about when the Franklin was hit?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, the captain on there--in the front of that book is the four captains that were captains aboard the Santa Fe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: It is clear to the front. You probably missed it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Here we go. Yeah. The captains of the Santa Fe; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. It was the third captain there that--Fitz.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fitz?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Who took her alongside the Franklin. He brought her in and he actually almost rammed it. He came in and, God, we thought he was going to ram. But he backed her down and we just glided right into her. And the quartermaster, the captain told him what course; and he repeated it to Fitz. Fitz says, "Can't you hear? I told you what." And he chewed them out because they didn't believe him when he gave them orders for heading into the Franklin. And he brought that in there so slick. And we thought, Boy, this is going to be a hell of a collision. But he started backing her down when the bow was at the stern and we just kind of glided right in. And there is many pictures of the Franklin that is in that book.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So let me see if I remember this. That kept the Franklin from capsizing then?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No, it didn't keep her from capsizing. She did. She didn't--most of her damage was fire above the waterline, not below. And they got that all out. They had a lot of explosions. In fact, when we were right there alongside, she had an explosion up above the bridge. And you can see in the picture there is a lot of debris. And when that explosion was, on the Santa Fe you can hear stuff hit the deck. There was particles of metal. And I was in charge of the breeches buoy. And we rigged the breeches buoy over and was taking the wounded over. There was about actually 700 and something men from the Franklin came aboard our ship. And there was a lot of them that were in bad shape. I know one we had a stretcher where a guy's leg was probably almost severed off. And somebody says, "Are you going to get up and walk out?" I said, "Hey, what are you talking about? This guy ain't got a leg here." But it was very hairy, you know, because we didn't know what the heck was going to happen, was she going to blow again or something. But we took her back to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So this left a skeleton crew on the Franklin?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. There was quite a few left on it. I don't know how many. There must have quite a few killed on there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Eight hundred or something?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. There was a lot killed on there. And they took 700 or so off and on board our ship. So I don't know. I would imagine there was about 3200 men on the whole ship at that time. That is about what they carried.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you escorted the Franklin back to Pearl?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Then the Franklin went back to New York, didn't it?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Right. Uh-huh. I don't think they done anything. They never brought her back--never fixed her and brought her back. They didn't ever expect her to come back, but she came back on her own power.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It is known as the ship that wouldn't die; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. You don't see a lot of actual pictures in there when we were alongside, of what was happening. I think maybe the picture of that chaplain that was praying over that guy--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: --I think that is in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I have seen that. There is movie footage of that too; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when was the Franklin hit? That was '45 sometime?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, it was. We were up very close to Japan when she was hit. And we were really up in there--you know, it was towards the end of the war. And I know we had a lot of frames knocked out and we had, when we went alongside the Franklin. We went back to Long Beach and they repaired us, and we went back out. And it wasn't too long after that that the war was over. I think that was about--the action we was in. Thomas Swope:: Was the Franklin hit done mostly by Kamikazes or was it a combination of--

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I think it was the Kamikaze and a combination of the bombs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bombs?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was the Franklin hit? Roughly where was that? That must be in there somewhere; right? That was not near Okinawa or was it--the Franklin?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No. As I recall, we were up towards the Kyushu.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Up in there somewhere.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It wasn't near Ulithi, was it?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ulithi?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Franklin rescue. Okay. It says here, "Okinawa Operation, March '45."

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So somewhere in there.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: We were up--Ulithi, that was already secure in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then after that were you part of the occupying forces in Japan?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: When the war was over and they were signing on the Missouri, we went into Sasebo. We had an admiral aboard. And he was negotiating with an admiral in Sasebo. We were there about a week. And I had shipped over once during the war. I figured I could ship over two more years, see. So another boatswain's mate that I knew in the First and Second Division, he had shipping over leave. And all of that came out that you could take your leave right now. So he said, "Well, let's take our leave." So I got off in Sasebo and came back on a destroyer escort which was one of these demolition ships. It had frogmen aboard. I went back to San Francisco and took my thirty days leave and come back out there. And I took 170 something men up to Adak, Alaska, and was in charge of them on a transport. I was a second class boatswain's mate then. And at Adak they had three 90-foot seagoing tubs there. And this commander up on the hill, we went up to see him. And he says, "Take your pick." And, you know, Adak is a muddy hell hole. They say there is a woman behind every tree up there; but there are no trees, you know. So I says, "I don't want no part of this." So I guess it worked. And I flew from there to Kodiak and went aboard a salvage ship, the ARS-21. It was about a 60 man crew, the same type of ship that picked up over in the east the Kennedy kid, you know, like the Grapple and I forget what the other one is--that type of ship. We had divers aboard. We only had one diver, but we had a diving locker. I was in charge of that. After being aboard, that captain made me first class just like that. And we had a couple of rescue jobs up there where a ship run aground and we took women and children off and then the men last. And it was--we had been into Valdez four or five times. And at that time there was nothing there but a wooden dock. There were three bars there and about eleven or twelve hundred people. In the winter they don't do nothing but get drunk and drink. And after that we came back down to Astoria, Oregon. We docked at the Columbia River for a couple of days and down to San Diego. There was a lot of destroyers down there. We towed from there up to Bremerton, Washington. And we would tow three at one crack. She had a lot of power. And she had a towing cable. You could let a lot of scope out and just pull the cable and everything that was on it would come. And each one of them destroyers was hooked up. All we did was hook up one and the others came. And we done that about two or three times. We were back in San Pedro, and my time was up. They were going to take the Curb out of commission in Boston. She was going through the canal that way. Well, my time was up and I was still aboard. And I thought, "Jeeze, if I go to stay aboard, I am going to go through the canal and go up to Boston." So the old man finally let me go. But he tried to get me to ship over, and I wasn't interested. I had met my wife in Seattle and we were going to get married. And, of course, I was down in San Diego and San Pedro and back up. And she waited for me. And then when I got out, I got a train. Of course, you didn't fly then; you took a train. And I went up. And we got married up there by--her uncles were all attorneys. She had a couple of them. And one was a superior court judge. And she also worked for him as a recorder. And so one of them married us up us in Seattle. And she worked at the Ben Franklin at the desk. And the manager and his wife stood up for us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you enjoy your life on the sea, on board ship?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I liked the water. Yes, I enjoyed it. Sometimes I didn't. But I had no qualms about being in the Navy, and I am glad I did spend that time in the Navy. It was one heck of an experience. You would have got nowhere the experience we had. And, of course, the war gave you a hell of a lot more experience. And it was--I would say it was a hell of an education. I spent time on four ships. Two of them sunk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much entertainment on board ship?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, on board ship during the war, whenever you could get in somewhere where there was no enemy, you had a movie. That is about the size of your entertainment, is a movie.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what did you do to pass the time between actions?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, between actions, you know, like on the Santa Fe, I was in charge up on the boat deck. And you were cleaning, you were painting, you were cleaning, and painting. And, you know, that salt would rust everything, you know. And you were chipping and painting. And we worked with canvas, leather, sewing and different things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Backtracking to Pearl Harbor, you were probably below deck when the Arizona was hit; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No. I didn't even know she was hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't feel the explosion or anything?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No, I didn't know anything. And I don't think we even felt anything. Being in the turret, every time we were hit, I thought we were firing the guns. And I was wondering why they weren't calling for shells. But they weren't firing the guns; we were being hit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind about your World War II experiences?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: You know, there is probably many, but I can't think of them, you know, offhand. There was a lot of different incidents. You would have to bring them out of me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was never in the Navy and I certainly wasn't in World War II.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Do you want to talk about girls?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Let's talk about girls. There certainly weren't any girls on the ship. Did you get to see many girls?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, you know, when I went in--and really out of six years, I was almost out to sea for five. And somebody said, "Well, you had a lot of girlfriends." I said, "Bullshit." I said, "Are you talking about mermaids? I didn't see any."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how long was it before you actually were able to see your family? I mean from the beginning of the war until--

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Let's see. I never came back until after we were sunk on the Astoria. Then I got 30 days leave.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I came back. And then after going on the Santa Fe and going back to Philadelphia, I snuck home because that coming to Cleveland wasn't too bad. And I got a long weekend and I came home, and I was just a couple of days home. And then let me see, one other time I got home. But that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Let's see. Okay. One time I come from Seattle-- I can't think of it--yeah, and I flew. The first time I ever flew. And one time I came home from Los Angeles and I hitchhiked home and back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's a long ride.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. At that time you could hitchhike. People would pick you up if you were a sailor, you know, in the service. And if you wanted to go and just sleep in their car and not stop, you could come across the country, you know, in three days. And it took that much--three and a half days--to come on the train. Now, you know, the thing about them trains, they are what we call them "milk trains." They are always stopping and going, stopping. I would love to make a trip across on one of these trains now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Of course, they are not stopping, only certain places, and everything is different. It is like going on a cruise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not the same kind of cruises you took, huh?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I don't--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't know anything else specific to ask you. You know, whatever you want to tell me about life in the Navy that you haven't told me already.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Well, life, if you weren't in combat, one thing that out there, it seemed like we lost an awful lot of sleep. We were at our battle stations an awful lot. And, you know, they were picking up stuff. Maybe they wouldn't ever come in, but they were picking up stuff on the radar. The Santa Fe, when she went out, she had the latest of everything. Like, we were up in the Aleutians. They had what they called the Battle of the Sitka Pip. What it was was that they were firing on the clouds. And I think it was Admiral Kincaid told Burke, "I said, 'Fire.'" He said there was nothing out there. And there wasn't. We never fired a shot. But all the other ships were firing at this pip, and it was bouncing off a cloud. And they had older radar. And our ship never picked up anything out there. And there is a story about this, and they call it The Battle of the Sitka Pip.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess it was picking up an echo off a cloud.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the California eventually capsize?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It just kind of sunk; right?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: It settled down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: And we put out all the cable and all the lines and then they put the anchor chain around because they thought maybe she would go over. They brought her back, reconstructed her--new superstructure and everything--and she was back out there. She was in that, in the Philippine battle, where they were firing on them Japanese battleships down there with the Tennessee, the West Virginia. Oh, it was the old battleships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: And we were up there with Halsey chasing that, it was supposed to be, a carrier group. And Nimitz was saying, "Where are you, Halsey?" He was aboard the New Jersey, the Missouri, and all of these new battleships. He should have been down there. They could have annihilated them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was in Midway you were going after that other force?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: That was way late in the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was late in the war?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Around the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right. I just saw something on the History Channel where Halsey thought that they were--yes, and he took the bait.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. Now this Burke, Admiral Burke, became a four-star. And he said he knew Halsey. He came to some of our reunions. And he used to say Halsey was a dumb ass. He took us in that typhoon. Jesus Christ, it was bad. We lost three destroyers and practically all the crews on them three destroyers. One of the carrier's bow bashed in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was that like going through that typhoon?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Oh, Jesus Christ. You couldn't stand up and eat or anything. We had--it shows in that book how many degrees we listed. It is a wonder we didn't roll over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I think Halsey ended up taking the fleet through a second typhoon later.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in the typhoon that was near Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We were in two of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think you are right. I have seen pictures of the carrier that was bent down like that.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I am trying to think what carrier that was. Anyway, I got a friend over here that was on that carrier.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: Yeah. But I didn't know it until later. I went to school with him. He said, "Why the hell didn't you wave at me?" Yeah. He showed me a picture of it. He has a book?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that the Essex?

sp.speaker: Eugene Hardy
sp.p: I think so. I think so. Yeah. (Interview concluded abruptly with no conclusion indicated by the interviewer.)
